# Model-based meta-analysis: start here

A model-based meta-analysis (MBMA) fits a model to published summary data: one
mean per trial arm and visit, each with its standard error and arm size. ferx
supports it through several features, each documented on its own reference page.
This page lists them in the order you meet them when you build such a model, and
links to the section that holds the details.

## Maturity

Every piece below is **beta**: θ level blocks, `profile`, nested levels,
within-arm residual correlation, residual and kappa `weight =`, and
compartment-free models. Each is marked so at the top of its own section, and
each has a row in the
[MBMA group of the Feature Maturity table](../maturity.qmd#model-based-meta-analysis-mbma-features)
naming the NONMEM anchor behind the label. Several pieces are limited to
`method = foce` or `focei`; where a step is limited, it says so.

## A minimal model

The pieces fit together like this. The model is ferx-core's
`tests/data/mbma_placebo/mbma_placebo.ferx` (the same model ferx-r bundles as
`mbma_placebo`), with the optional `profile` and `correlation` additions marked:

```
[parameters]
  theta TVE0(45.0, 0.0, 200.0)      # mean placebo level over a study's visits
  theta EMAX(8.0, 0.0, 100.0)       # maximum drug effect
  theta ED50(20.0, 0.1, 1000.0)     # dose at half-maximal effect
  theta ET50(2.0, 0.01, 100.0)      # time to half-maximal drug effect
  theta PLACEBO[STUDY, TIME, contrast = sum_to_zero_within](0.0, -50.0, 50.0) profile  # `profile` optional
  theta RHO(0.3, 0.0, 0.95)         # optional: only with the correlation line

  omega ETA_E0 ~ 4.0 (sd)           # between-study variability
  kappa KAPPA_ARM ~ 4.0 (sd) weight = NARM   # between-arm variability (BTAV)

  sigma ADD_ERR ~ 1.0 (variance) FIX         # all precision is in the weight

[covariates]
  STUDY categorical
  NARM  continuous
  SE    continuous
  DOSE  continuous

[individual_parameters]
  BASE = TVE0 + PLACEBO + ETA_E0 + KAPPA_ARM

[structural_model]
  DRUG = EMAX * DOSE / (ED50 + DOSE) * TIME / (TIME + ET50)
  y    = BASE - DRUG

[error_model]
  DV ~ additive(ADD_ERR) weight = SE
  correlation car1(RHO) by OCC      # optional

[fit_options]
  method     = focei
  iov_column = OCC
  covariance = true
```

Without the `profile` keyword and the two optional lines it is the fixture as
committed. With them it parses with `ferx check` and fits on the fixture's data.

## 1. Arm-level data

Each row is one arm of one study at one visit. `ID` is the study, an occasion
column (`OCC`, named by `iov_column`) is the arm, and `DV` is the reported arm
mean on its natural scale. The arm's standard error and size are ordinary data
columns (`SE`, `NARM` above). In the MBMA layout the arms of a study are its
occasions, and each arm carries the study's visit grid
([Kappas](parameters.qmd#kappas)). See [Required Columns](../data-format.qmd#required-columns)
and [Occasion Column (IOV)](../data-format.qmd#occasion-column-iov).

There are no dose records. The model is a
[compartment-free model](structural-model.qmd#compartment-free-models-the-pred-equivalent):
a `[structural_model]` with no `pk` or `ode` line, whose `y = ...` equation reads
the dose as a data column. The dataset needs no `AMT` column, and dose records it
carries anyway are not applied
([What a compartment-free model does not have](structural-model.qmd#what-a-compartment-free-model-does-not-have)).
A kappa on such a model keeps the analytic gradient up to 48 random effects per
subject, counting the stacked η and kappas over its occasions; past that, the fit
uses finite differences ([Gradients](structural-model.qmd#gradients)).

In R, `ferx_mbma_data()` builds and checks such a dataset
([Counted form](parameters.qmd#counted-form-theta-namen)).

## 2. Inverse-variance weighting

Add `weight = SE` to the error-model line and fix the additive sigma at 1:
each row then contributes $1/SE^2$ to the objective, and `DV`, `PRED`, the sdtab
and the VPC stay on the natural scale
([Residual weighting](error-model.qmd#residual-weighting-weight-...)). Whether
sigma is fixed stays your choice: fix it for a continuous endpoint with a known
SE, estimate it for a weighted logit of a proportion
([Is sigma fixed?](error-model.qmd#is-sigma-fixed)). The reported OFV differs
from a hand-built `DV/SE` fit by a constant that cancels from every ΔOFV
([Objective-function value](error-model.qmd#objective-function-value)).

## 3. Between-arm variability

`kappa KAPPA_ARM ~ 4.0 (sd) weight = NARM` declares an arm random effect with
variance $\gamma^2 / N$, so a large arm's mean varies less than a small arm's
([Sample-size-weighted IOV](iov.qmd#sample-size-weighted-iov-weight-...)). The
estimate reported is the unweighted $\gamma^2$, and the fit prints the SD at the median
arm size on the next line ([What is reported](iov.qmd#what-is-reported)). The
weight may read covariates, `FIX`ed thetas and `TIME`, and the kappa may be read
only in `[individual_parameters]` ([Rules and diagnostics](iov.qmd#rules-and-diagnostics)).

## 4. Placebo time course as a level block

`theta PLACEBO[STUDY, TIME](...)` declares one fixed effect per (study, visit)
cell in the data, so no parametric placebo curve is imposed
([Theta level blocks](parameters.qmd#theta-level-blocks),
[Data-driven form](parameters.qmd#data-driven-form-theta-namecol-...)). Next to
an intercept and a study random effect, one degree of freedom per study has to
go. `contrast = sum_to_zero_within`, the default for this shape, makes the
levels sum to zero within each study
([Identifiability](parameters.qmd#identifiability)). `TVE0 + ETA_E0` is then
each study's mean placebo level over its own visits, and the levels are each
visit's deviation from it. A block of 20 or more coefficients is summarised rather
than listed in the estimate table; the derived level of each study is not a
coefficient and does not count ([Fitting at this scale](parameters.qmd#fitting-at-this-scale)).

## 5. Profiled level blocks

Marking the block `profile` takes its levels out of the optimizer's search: at
every outer evaluation they are solved exactly for the structural parameters being
tried. The objective is unchanged, so the OFV, the estimates and a likelihood-ratio
test agree with the unprofiled fit
([Profiled level blocks](parameters.qmd#profiled-level-blocks)). It pays off when
the block has many levels; on a small model it can be slower
([When to profile](parameters.qmd#when-to-profile)). The block must enter every
prediction linearly, under `foce`/`focei` at `n_agq = 1` with an additive,
untransformed Gaussian error and no M3
([When it applies](parameters.qmd#when-it-applies)). A profiled block takes bounds,
and a level held on its bound gets no standard error
([Bounds on a profiled block](parameters.qmd#bounds-on-a-profiled-block)). `r`,
`s` and `rsr` all work on a profiled fit
([Standard errors](parameters.qmd#standard-errors)).

## 6. Nested levels

For sponsor → study → arm, put the coarsest grouping in `ID` and declare the finer
ones with `level NAME by COLUMN in PARENT`, then attach each kappa with
`kappa ... at LEVEL` ([Nested levels](iov.qmd#nested-levels),
[Declaring levels](iov.qmd#nested-levels-declaring)). A `level` replaces
`iov_column`. Every record needs a numeric label at every level
([The data](iov.qmd#nested-levels-data)). Nested levels are estimated with
`foce` or `focei` at `n_agq = 1` only
([What this release supports](iov.qmd#nested-levels-scope)).

## 7. Within-arm residual correlation

`correlation cs|ar1|car1(RHO) by ARM` lets the residuals of one arm's visits
correlate ([Within-group residual correlation](residual-correlation.qmd)). It is
fitted by `foce` and `focei` only ([Scope](residual-correlation.qmd#scope)). `cs`
and an arm kappa are the same covariance, so `cs` over the groups of a
kappa-carrying level is refused; with a kappa at the arm, use `ar1` or `car1`
([With kappa and nested levels](residual-correlation.qmd#with-kappa-and-nested-levels),
[Choosing a structure](residual-correlation.qmd#choosing-a-structure)). The line
fits next to a profiled level block, and its refusals come first
([With a profiled level block](residual-correlation.qmd#with-a-profiled-level-block)).

With few studies, do not read the OFV drop for `ρ` against a χ² distribution.
On the 6-study `mbma_placebo` data, which the generator draws with no serial
correlation, `car1(RHO) by OCC` lowers the OFV by 7.6. In 50 data sets simulated
from the fit without the line (ferx-r
`ferx_simulate(model, data, n_sim = 50, seed = 1, fit = fit)`), each fitted with
and without it, the drop was at least 3.84 in 26% of them (macOS arm64, core
`32dbb309`). A χ²₁ reference puts 5% there; since `ρ ≥ 0` places the null on the
boundary of its range, the asymptotic reference is the 50:50 χ²₀/χ²₁ mixture,
which puts 2.5% there. Calibrate the test by simulating from the model without
the line, as the ferx book's MBMA chapter does in
[Correlated residuals within an arm](https://ferx-nlme.org/ferx-book/chapters/24-mbma.html#correlated-residuals-within-an-arm).

## 8. Uncertainty with few studies

The default `covariance_method = r` gives the model-based SEs
([Covariance estimator](../estimation/foce.qmd#covariance-estimator-r-s-or-sandwich)).
When the analytic R-matrix is out of scope and the model has more than 100 free
coordinates, a defaulted method routes to `s` with a warning; set
`covariance_method = r` to keep it
([Fitting at this scale](parameters.qmd#fitting-at-this-scale)).
`s` needs more subjects than free parameters, so a level block with a level per
study leaves `S` rank-deficient and `s` reports no SEs. On a block whose levels
are each read by one subject, the `rsr` level SEs are not usable; read them from
`r`, and ferx warns with `W_COV_RSR_ONE_SUBJECT_LEVELS`
([Standard errors](parameters.qmd#standard-errors)).

[SIR](../estimation/sir.qmd) (`sir = true`, beta) samples from the covariance
step's proposal. It never samples a `FIX`ed sigma, so the fixed residual of the
weighting stays fixed
([Rank-deficient and non-identified proposals](../estimation/sir.qmd#rank-deficient-and-non-identified-proposals)).
On the 6-study `mbma_placebo` fixture the default `sir_scale = packed` gives a
higher effective sample size than `natural`, whose target has a heavy upper tail
for a variance informed by few groups
([Choosing the target scale](../estimation/sir.qmd#choosing-the-target-scale)).
`covariance_fallback = sir` runs it when the Hessian is not positive definite
([SIR fallback](../estimation/foce.qmd#sir-fallback-for-non-pd-hessians)).

## 9. Bundled examples

- `examples/mbma_naproxen.ferx` with `data/mbma_naproxen.csv`: the published
  naproxen-versus-placebo MBMA of Boucher & Bennetts (2018), 18 trials and 36 arms,
  with between-study random effects and no kappa. It keeps the published
  weighting, written by hand: `DV` divided in the data, `y` divided by `WPSE`,
  sigma `FIX` at 1, the construction `weight =` replaces
  ([Replaces the hand-built three-site construction](error-model.qmd#replaces-the-hand-built-three-site-construction)).
  `data/mbma_naproxen.README.md` gives the provenance. **The data are licensed
  CC BY-NC 4.0, not MIT** (`data/mbma_naproxen.LICENSE`): commercial use is not
  granted.

  ```bash
  ferx examples/mbma_naproxen.ferx --data data/mbma_naproxen.csv
  ```

- `tests/data/mbma_placebo/`: the synthetic model above, with data. ferx-r bundles it as
  `ferx_example("mbma_placebo")`, and the ferx book's
  [MBMA chapter](https://ferx-nlme.org/ferx-book/chapters/24-mbma.html) works
  through it end to end from R.

  ```bash
  ferx tests/data/mbma_placebo/mbma_placebo.ferx --data tests/data/mbma_placebo/mbma_placebo.csv
  ```
